Sitting on top of this concretion were three anchors and three bronze guns. The three guns have been lifted and are being conserved by the National Museum of Ireland.

…the rudder of the vessel overlying another bronze gun with lifting dolphins (Fig. 6).

I have not done so until now that God has brought me to these States of Flanders, where I arrived twelve days ago with the Spaniards who escaped from the ships that were lost in Ireland,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: where I arrived twelve days ago with the Spaniards who escaped from the ships that were lost in Ireland, Scotland, and Shetland, which were more than twenty of the largest in the Armada.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: being more than two hundred, not five survived;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and with me three hundred and odd soldiers, who also knew how to save themselves and to swim to shore.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: passing more than seven months among mountains and woods with savages,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: After the fierce engagement we had off Calais on the 8th of August, continuing from the morning till seven o'clock in the evening—
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: our Armada being in the act of retiring—oh! I don't know how I can say it—the fleet of our enemy followed behind to drive us from their country; and when it was accomplished, and everything was safe, which was on the 10th of the same [month],
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: a pilot, a bad man whom I had, without saying anything to me, had made sail and passed out in advance of the admiral's ship for about two miles,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: a tender came alongside and summoned me, on the part of the Duke, to go on board the admiral's ship. I proceeded thither;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: He ordered me to be taken to the ship of the Judge Advocate General,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: scattered in such manner by the storm that some ships went to Germany, others drove on the islands of Holland and Zealand into the enemies' hands, others went to Shetland, others to Scotland,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: As I have said, the ship I sailed in was from the Levant, to which were attached two others, very large, to afford us aid if they could.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and not being able to weather Cape Clear (?), in Ireland, on account of the severe storm which arose upon the bow, he was forced to make for the land with these three ships,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and to anchor more than half a league from the shore,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: where we remained for four days without being able to make any provision,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: On the fifth [day] there sprang up so great a storm on our beam,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and we were driven ashore with all three ships upon a beach, covered with very fine sand, shut in on one side and the other by great rocks.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: for within the space of an hour all three ships were broken in pieces,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: so that there did not escape three hundred men, and more than one thousand were drowned,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: Thereupon more than seventy men, who had remained alive, jumped from the ship to the boat, and while she was making for the land so great a wave washed over her that she sank, and all on deck were swept away. Then she drifted along, rolling over in different directions with the waves, until she went ashore, where she settled wrong side up,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: More than a day and a half after she had grounded, some savages arrived, who turned her up for the purpose of extracting nails or pieces of iron;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I say that I placed myself on the top of the poop of my ship,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: who went about jumping and dancing with delight at our misfortunes; and when any one of our people reached the beach, two hundred savages and other enemies fell upon him and stripped him of what he had on until he was left in his naked skin. Such they maltreated and wounded without pity, all of which was plainly visible from the battered ships,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and when any one of our people reached the beach, two hundred savages and other enemies fell upon him and stripped him of what he had on until he was left in his naked skin.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: as I did not know how to swim,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: which was to take the cover of a hatchway, about as large as a good-sized table, that by chance the mercy of God brought to my hand. When I tried to place myself upon it, it sank with me to a depth of six times my height below the surface,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: When I came up again,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: there came a huge wave, breaking over us in such a manner that the Judge Advocate was unable to resist it, and the wave bore him away and drowned him,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and at that moment a piece of timber crushed my legs.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: there came four waves, one after the other, and, without knowing how, or knowing how to swim, they cast me upon the shore,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: where I emerged, unable to stand, all covered with blood,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: did not touch me nor approach me, seeing me, as I have said, with my legs and hands and my linen trousers covered with blood.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: In this condition I proceeded, little by little, as I could, meeting many Spaniards stripped to the skin,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: which would be about nine o'clock at night, the wind was calm and the sea subsiding.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: cut a quantity of rushes and grass, covered us well, and then betook themselves to the shore to plunder and break open money- chests and whatever they might find, at which work more than two thousand savages and Englishmen,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: at about one o'clock in the night, I was disturbed by a great noise of men on horseback—there were more than two hundred of them—
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I turned to call my companion, to see if he slept, and found he was dead,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: There he lay on the ground with more than six hundred other dead bodies which the sea cast up,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and the crows and wolves* devoured them,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: At the dawn of day I began to walk, little by little, searching for a monastery of monks,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: searching for a monastery of monks, that I might might recover in it, as best I could, which I arrived at with much trouble and toil. I found it deserted, and the church and images of the saints burned and completely ruined, and twelve Spaniards hanging within the church by the act of the Lutheran English,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and betook myself to a road which lay through a great wood. When I had gone by it for the matter of a mile,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I met with a woman of more than eighty years of age, a rough savage, who was carrying off five or six cows to hide them in that wood,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I decided to go to the shore, where the ships lay that were wrecked three days before,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: There were stretched out upon that strand more than four hundred, among whom we recognised some, and the poor Don Diego Enriquez, whom, with all my sad plight, I did not wish to pass by without burying him in a pit, which we made in the sand, at the water's edge.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and he may have been a chief, for they respected him. This man, by the grace of God, assisted me and my two companions, and brought us away from there, and remained a good while in our company, until he put us on a road which led from the coast to a village where he lived.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: that road was very stony, and I was unable to move or go a step forward, because I went shoeless, and dying with pain in one of my legs,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and reached a height, from whence I discovered some huts of straw; and going towards them by a valley,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I entered a wood. When I had gone a distance of two shots of an arquebus in it,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: one English, the other French—and a girl of the age of twenty years, most beautiful in the extreme, who were all going to the shore to plunder.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and cut the sinew of my right leg. He wanted to repeat the blow immediately, had not the savage come up with his daughter, who may have been this Englishman's friend,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: under which I wore a gold chain of the value of rather more than a thousand dollars. When they saw it, they rejoiced greatly, and searched the jacket, thread by thread, in which I carried forty-five crown-pieces in gold, that the Duke had ordered to be given to me at Corunna for two months' pay;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: From her hut they sent me a boy with a poultice made of herbs, to put upon my wound, and butter and milk and a small piece of oaten bread to eat.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: The person who did me this service was born a Frenchman, who had been a soldier at Terceira,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: he told me to continue travelling straight towards some mountains that appeared to be about six leagues off, behind which there were good lands belonging to an important savage very friendly to the King of Spain; and that he gave shelter to, and treated well, all the Spaniards who went to him; and that he had in his village more than eighty of those from the ships who reached there naked.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I began to walk as best I could, making for the direction of the mountains,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: That night I reached some huts, where they did not do me harm, because there was in them one who knew Latin;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: middle of the night his father arrived and his brothers, loaded with plunder and our things,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: In the morning they gave me a horse and a boy to convey me over a mile of bad road that there was, with mud up to the girths.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: They would be about one hundred and fifty horsemen going back to the coast to plunder as many Spaniards as they found.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: He took me away to hide in some rugged places among the rocks,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: there fell in with me more than forty savages on foot,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: for two of those robbers came up to me and gave me six blows of a stick, which bruised my shoulders and arms, and they stripped me of everything that I wore, so as to leave me as naked as when I was born.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and with some bracken leaves and a small piece of old matting which I wrapped around my body,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: reaching the mountain range that they gave me for direction, I met with a lake, around which there were about thirty huts, all forsaken and unoccupied,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: Eleven of us were stripped together at the shore, and in this naked state we came to seek some land of Christians. On the way, there met us a party of enemies, who killed eight of us, and the three who are here made our escape through a wood so thick that they could not discover us.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and that I brought word of a village, which was three or four leagues distant, that belonged to Señor de Ruerque [O'Rourke],
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: there came to the door a savage, with a halberd in his hand, and he began to look at his oats and to talk to himself. [...] We remained quiet, buried alive,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed; two nearby passages joined, the gap marked [...]

verbatim.text: while we awaited the rising of the moon.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: we sallied forth from that great danger, in which we had been, without waiting for the day.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: stumbling in the mud, and dying with hunger, thirst, and pain, until God was pleased to bring us to a land of some safety, where we found huts of better people,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: In it I met with more than seventy Spaniards, who all went about naked and severely maltreated,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: because the chief was not there. He had gone to defend a territory which the English were coming to take;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: news was told us that a Spanish ship was at the coast, that she was very large, and came for those Spaniards who had escaped.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: the whole twenty of us left for the direction where they told us the ship was,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: they set sail from thence in two days with the crew that came in her and those they had picked up, returning, to run aground and get wrecked, on the same coast. More than two hundred persons were drowned,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: It pleased God that I alone remained of the twenty who went in search of her,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and he directed me by the right road that I should go to reach a castle, which was six leagues from there.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: took me to his hut in a deserted valley, where he said I must live all my life, and he would teach me his trade, which was that of a blacksmith. I did not know what to answer nor did I venture*, so that he should not put me in the forge. Before him I showed a pleasant countenance, and proceeded to work with my bellows for more than eight days,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: a Spanish soldier, of whom he had already ten with him of those who had escaped by swimming.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and I remained there three months, acting as a real savage like themselves.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: The custom of these savages is to live as the brute beasts among the mountains, which are very rugged in that part of Ireland where we lost ourselves. They live in huts made of straw.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and do not let them enter their territory, which is subject to inundation, and marshy. That district extends for more than forty leagues in length and breadth.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: no other remedy but to withdraw themselves to the mountains, with their women and cattle;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: Word of this reached the great Governor of the Queen, who was in the city of Duplin [Dublin],
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: with seventeen hundred soldiers, to search for the lost ships and the people who had escaped.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: They were not much fewer than one thousand men, who, without arms and naked, were wandering about the country in the locality where each ship had been lost.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: marched with them along the whole of the coasts till he arrived at the place where I was wrecked. From thence he turned off towards the castle of Manglana [MacClancy],
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: This savage, taking into consideration the great force that was coming against him, and that he could not resist it, decided to fly to the mountains,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: the nine Spaniards who were there, would cheerfully remain in it and defend it to the death.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: for it is founded in a lake of very deep water, which is more than a league wide at some parts, and three or four leagues long, and has an outlet to the sea;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: with the rise of spring tides it is not possible to enter it,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: because fo] a league round the town, which is established on the mainland, it is marshy, breast-deep,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: about eighteen hundred men—and observed us from a distance of a mile and a half from it,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and hanged two Spaniards, and did other injuries to put us in fear. He demanded many times, by a trumpeter, that we should surrender the castle,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: We had been besieged for seventeen days, when our Lord saw fit to succour and deliver us from that enemy by severe storms and great falls of snow,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: which took place to such an extent that he [the Queen's Governor] was compelled to depart with his force, and to march back to Duplin [Dublin],
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: but contented myself with a guide to direct me to a place where I could meet with embarkation for Scotland.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: to depart one morning two hours before dawn, so that they should not pursue us on the road: [...] with the four soldiers, one morning ten days after the Nativity, in the year 1588.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed; two nearby passages joined, the gap marked [...]

verbatim.text: I travelled by the mountains and desolate places, enduring much hardship, as God knows; and at the end of twenty days' journey,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I got to the place where Alonzo de Leyva, and the Count de Paredes and Don Tomas de Granvela, were lost,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: until one day I heard of the territory of a savage, whom they called Prince Ocan, where there were some vessels that were going to Scotland.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: The vessels had left two days before,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: so much so that in no manner could I stand upon it.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: Some women, when they saw me alone, and ill, pitied me, and took me away to their little huts on the mountain, and kept me there for more than a month and a half in safety, and cured me,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and I felt well enough to go to Ocan's village to speak with him. But he did not wish to hear or see me; for, it was said, he had given his word to the great Governor of the Queen not to keep any Spaniard in his territory,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: The English, who were quartered there, having marched off to invade a territory and take it, Ocan accompanied them with all his force,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and that I should have to go with them to the city of Dublin,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and I did so in great haste, leaping banks as I went along. I got among thick brambles,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: I had arrived at a very large laguna [lake or marsh], along the banks of which I saw a herd of cows walking,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: They came to collect their cows, and take them up the mountain to where they and their fathers were hiding for fear of the English; and there I spent two days with them, being treated with much kindness. One of the boys had to go to the village of the Prince of Ocan to ascertain what news or rumour there was,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: so that I had to leave there very early in the morning,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and to go in search of a bishop, who was seven leagues off in a castle where the English kept him in banishment and retirement.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: This bishop was a very good Christian, and went about in the garb of a savage for concealment, and I assure you I could not restrain tears when I approached him to kiss his hand. He had twelve Spaniards with him for the purpose of passing them over to Scotland,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: He treated me with every kindness that he could for the six days I was with him, and gave orders that a boat should come to take us over to Scotland,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: That same day at dawn,* I went to sea in a wretched boat in which we sailed— 18 persons—
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: and the wind becoming contrary the same day, we were forced to run before it, at the mercy of God, for Shetland, where we reached the land at daylight;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: in two days, with good weather, we left for Scotland, where we arrived in three days:
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: as we were left for more than six months as naked as when we arrived from Ireland,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: There was a Scotch merchant in Flanders, who offered and agreed with his Highness that he would come to Scotland for us and ship us in four vessels, with the provisions which were necessary, and that he would bring us to Flanders, his Highness giving him five ducats for each Spaniard of those that he brought to Flanders.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: which the Dutch did as they were commanded; and were on the look-out for us for a month and a half at the said port of Dunkirk,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: God willed that of the four vessels in which we came, two escaped and grounded, where they went to pieces;
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: we cast ourselves afloat on timbers, and some soldiers were drowned, as was also a Scotch captain. I reached the shore in my shirt,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: the Dutch making a thousand pieces of two hundred and seventy Spaniards who came in the ship which brought us to Dunkirk,
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

verbatim.text: From the City of Antwerp, 4th October, 1589.
verbatim.note: Crawford's English, not Cuéllar's Spanish; running page headers removed

subject: src:ship-lavia

statement.observable: mass of Lavia's wreck on the seabed (ballast mound, lower hull, metal, guns and cargo), once the site is surveyed; and her ballast mound alone
statement.stated_before: 2026-11-07; no ballast mound or timber extent measured at Streedagh

lwl_over_esloria.basis: esloria is the main-deck length from stem to sternpost (Martin p. 409). The waterline lies between that and the keel, which Martin takes as 53/65 of the esloria for Lavia, after Veitia Linage's 700-ton galleon (App. 1 n. 5, p. 506)

bwl_over_manga.basis: manga is the beam taken internally at midships (p. 409); add frames and planking on both sides, less any narrowing at the waterline

normal_draught_over_puntal.basis: the draught fully laden. Puntal runs from under the main deck to the bottom of the hold (p. 409). Martin's draughts: Valencera about 4 m normal (p. 130), Girona about 4.5 m (p. 174), San Juan de Sicilia about 20 ft from her 28 ft rudder (p. 217). For Lavia's 6.18 m puntal this range gives 4.0-5.9 m

block_coeff.basis: full-bodied Mediterranean merchant hulls; no lines survive. The rating formula's own (M/2) x 0.97 treats the hold as 0.485 of its box: a hint, not evidence

lightship_frac.basis: hull, rig, ground tackle and fittings as a share of the fully laden displacement. No surviving figure for these hulls: the leading open question (see drivers)

rig_share.basis: masts, yards, sails and cordage as a share of the lightship

metal_share.basis: iron in the lightship: bolts and fastenings (these Levant hulls were iron-fastened, Martin p. 217), anchors, chain-plates, galley ironwork

ballast_scale.basis: multiplies the Rosa's 90 t (p. 150) at 945 toneladas (p. 139), scaled by machos as a volume proxy. Wide: the mound is what survived, and ballasting varied

cargo_u.basis: position in each ship's cargo range (CARGO_T), shared: siege train and army stores beyond the ship's own munitions

liquid_days.basis: days of wine and water left. Six months' rations at Lisbon, replenished at Corunna, 50% wastage allowed; it was the unintended voyage home without water that caused the privations (p. 349). The ships had put in to the Irish coast

solid_days.basis: days of biscuit, meat, fish, cheese, pulses, oil left (same basis)

cask_tare.basis: cask mass as a share of the liquid it holds (Valencera's restored pipa held about 591 l, p. 351)

person_t.basis: one person with clothing, in tonnes. In the displacement, not in the seabed mass

arms_kg_per_soldier.basis: arquebus or musket, morion, sword, bandolier, share of pikes

timber_retained.basis: share of hull timber that stayed on the seabed: the lower hull under the ballast (anchors and guns lie over the Site 1 concretion; the rudder over a gun), while castles, decks and upper works broke up and drove ashore (Cuellar's strand of timber)

rig_retained.basis: masts and spars float; wet cordage and sails partly sink with the wreck

stores_retained.basis: full casks sit near neutral buoyancy; biscuit dissolves

cargo_retained.basis: siege cargo is mostly dense (battery guns, shot, ironwork); the wheels, planks and baulks float

statement.note: median with 5-95% interval; people excluded (war grave); layer 1 included

inferences.falsifier: a measured ballast mound outside the 5-95% range, or lower-hull timber extent implying a seabed mass outside it; or an issue list showing cargo beyond 60 t

Three ships anchor off Streedagh
Ships driven ashore and broken within an hour
Calm by about 21:00
About 200 horsemen ride past at about 01:00 without seeing him
Walks inland at dawn to the burned monastery
Back at the strand where the ships 'were wrecked three days before'; buries Don Diego
Stony road; leg wound; huts in the wood
Night at the huts of the Latin-speaker
Horse and boy at morning; 150 horsemen; stripped naked
Reaches the lake with about 30 empty huts; night in the oat hut
Daybreak; buried in straw all day while reapers work outside
Nightfall; 'awaited the rising of the moon'; leave before day
Huts of 'better people'; kept until fit; then O'Rourke's village
'Early next day' news of a Spanish ship; the twenty set out
Wandering; meets the clergyman; directed to a castle six leagues off
Taken to a blacksmith's hut; bellows for more than eight days
Clergyman returns; MacClancy sends for him 'the following day'
Leaves MacClancy's castle two hours before dawn
After 20 days' journey reaches the Girona wreck site
Hears of O'Cahan's vessels; reaches them two days late
Hidden in huts on the mountain more than six weeks
Flight from O'Cahan's village; night by a lake
Two days on the mountain with the cowherd boys; leaves very early
Reaches the bishop seven leagues off; six days with him
Puts to sea at dawn; driven to Shetland; lands at daylight
Leaves Shetland after two days; arrives in Scotland after three
Leaves Scotland after more than six months
Shipped past English ports to Dunkirk; wrecked at the bar; ashore in Flanders
